hints: Look first at the recipient, not the donor. A person with blood group A has anti-B antibodies in their plasma, so which donor antigen would be attacked?
A transfusion is unsafe when the recipient's antibody meets the matching antigen on the donor red cells. Check which donor groups carry the B antigen and which carry no B antigen.
walkthrough:
**Focus on the recipient with group A**

Think of this like lock and key. The recipient's plasma contains the weapon.

From the table, group A recipient has: A antigen on own cells, and anti-B antibody in plasma. That anti-B will attack any B antigen that enters.

**Test each possible donor against anti-B**

The rule is simple: if donor red cells have B antigen, the recipient's anti-B will cause agglutination, and that is unsafe.

Group A donor: A only, no B, so safe. Group O donor: neither A nor B, so safe. Group B donor: B only, so attacked. Group AB donor: A and B, so the B part is attacked.

**Pick the safe combination**

Only donor blood with no B antigen can be given to a group A person.

That leaves A and O.

options.A: AB is unsafe because AB red cells carry B antigen, which will be attacked by the recipient's anti-B antibodies.
options.B: Correct, both A and O lack B antigen, so the group A recipient's anti-B has nothing to attack.
options.C: B is unsafe because B red cells carry B antigen, which will react with the recipient's anti-B antibodies.
options.D: AB only is wrong because AB cells carry B antigen and will be agglutinated, and it also misses the two truly safe groups, A and O.
